stories.title: The Bad Old Days of Indian Firms
stories.description: Ajay describes the pre-1990s Indian firm as a 'loose coalition' where branch managers were demigods with immense discretion (like Robert Clive without email). This led to local corruption and lack of process, exemplified by the necessity of arguing with an Indian Airlines frontline employee who actually had the power to change things.

stories.title: The IT Revolution and the Imperial Firm
stories.description: In the 90s and 2000s, telecom and IT allowed HQs to centralize control. 'Robert Clive was now under the daily misery of surveillance.' This created the 'Imperial Firm'—efficient, scalable, but rigid and standardized, rolling out one process for the whole country.

stories.title: The Diversity of Kerala
stories.description: Ajay cites CMIE data showing that Kerala is best understood as three distinct homogeneous regions (North, Central, South), each with different characteristics. Treating it as one state misses this nuance.

stories.title: The Mobile Phone Statistic
stories.description: To illustrate India's diversity, Ajay points out that the fraction of females owning a mobile phone varies by 18x between the highest and lowest homogeneous regions in India. This reflects deep social and economic differences.

stories.title: Kit Kat and Maggi
stories.description: Ajay observes that Kit Kats in Japan are magical and diverse, while in the US they are 'horrible' and sugar-loaded. Similarly, Maggi tastes different in every country. He asks why Indian firms don't adapt their products similarly for the diverse regions of India.

stories.title: Bank of America in 1991
stories.description: Ajay recalls that in 1991, Bank of America's entire Indian operation was the size of a tiny US state branch. The market was too small then to justify complex, adaptive structures, but that has changed.

recommendations.comment: Recommended by Amit. Shrayana Bhattacharya's book uses the fandom of Shah Rukh Khan to explore the economic and social lives of Indian women. Amit calls it 'The Loneliness of the Indian Woman'.

recommendations.item: The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner
recommendations.comment: Mentioned by Amit as the inspiration for his episode titles (and Shrayana's book title). A classic by Alan Sillitoe.
Recommended by Ajay. He suggests re-reading it as an adult to appreciate it as the foundational text that 'invents the idea of India'.
Mentioned by Ajay as another example of Nehru writing from memory in prison.

core_ideas.description: The state is often the wrong unit of analysis for India. A better abstraction (proposed by CMIE) is ~100 'homogeneous regions', each consisting of ~7 contiguous districts with similar agro-climatic and socio-economic conditions.

Indian firms moved from chaotic/local (pre-90s) to imperial/centralized (post-90s). The next evolution must be 'adaptive'—combining central strategy/capital allocation with decentralized execution that respects local diversity.
Amit warns against blindly applying global best practices (or 'imperial' standards) to local contexts where they don't fit, a concept from biology applied to institutions.
The richest homogeneous region in India is about 5 times richer than the poorest. This economic disparity demands differentiated business strategies.
India is more diverse than the combined continents of Latin America and Africa (according to Lant Pritchett). Treating it as a single market with a single product is a mistake.
Referencing Ronald Coase, Ajay discusses why firms are internally 'Stalinist' (command and control) while externally market-based. He argues modern firms can be less Stalinist and more federated.
As the Indian market grows, the fixed costs of adapting products and processes for local regions become justifiable. Firms that fail to adapt will leave room for local competitors.
